prompt: The Alagoa plant's folder holds four files named like POP-salmoura_v3_FINAL_revisado.docx. What does the auditor need that the folder does not record?
hint: Think about what the folder knows about each file.

choices.text: Who approved which version, and when
choices.why: Right: approval is a fact about the past, and a DMS keeps it in the object beside the file; a folder keeps a name, a date and its permissions.

choices.text: Which file is newest by date of last change
choices.why: The folder does record that date, and the newest file is not necessarily the approved one.

choices.text: Who is allowed to open the folder
choices.why: Folder permissions are one of the three things the folder does know.

choices.text: The text of each procedure
choices.why: The text is inside each file; the folder holds it perfectly well. What is missing is the record around the text.

prompt: Put the history of POP-JF-PAS-004 in the order it happened in 2026.
hint: The line keeps working to the old version until the very last step.
items: Version 1.0 checked out by a quality analyst
Version 1.1 checked in as a draft
Returned from review, checked in again as 1.2
Approved by Cláudia and made version 2.0
Effective date reached: 2.0 in force, 1.0 superseded

prompt: Version 1.2 of the pasteurisation procedure is under review and carries the CURRENT label. Which version should the operators on line 2 be working to?
hint: Latest and approved are two different markers.

choices.text: 1.2, because it carries the CURRENT label
choices.why: CURRENT marks the latest version, and here the latest is a draft that nobody has approved.

choices.text: 1.1, the first draft of the change
choices.why: A draft is not an instruction, and 1.1 was already replaced by 1.2 inside the review loop.
Right: minor versions are drafts, and the line works to the last major version until a new one takes effect.

choices.text: 2.0, which the review will produce
choices.why: 2.0 does not exist yet; it is made at approval, and even then the line waits for the effective date.

prompt: To fix Alagoa without a DMS, Felipe proposes a strict naming rule: plant, process, version and status in every file name. Which problem does the rule leave untouched?
hint: Two people, one file, same afternoon.

choices.text: Telling a draft from an approved file
choices.why: The status in the name does tell them apart, as long as everybody follows the rule.

choices.text: Knowing which plant a procedure belongs to
choices.why: The plant is in the name under this rule; classification by one attribute is what a name handles.

choices.text: Sorting the procedures by process
choices.why: Putting the process in the name gives exactly that sort order in the folder.

choices.text: Two people editing the same file at once
choices.why: Right: a name does not lock a file. Check-out is what stops a second editor, and a naming rule has no such mechanism.

prompt: ISO 15489 treats a record as information created, received and kept as ___ of what an organisation did.
hint: The reason an inspector asks for it.

prompt: Batch L2711-0388 is made on 2 November 2027. Under Serra Alta's schedule, its certificate of analysis is kept for 5 years counted from the end of the year the batch was made. In which year does the certificate first become eligible for disposal?
hint: Find the end of the production year, then add the period.

prompt: The January 2032 disposal run reaches the certificate of batch L2603-0112, whose retention period has ended. Legal placed a hold on it in 2031 and has not lifted it. What does the run do?
hint: Which wins, the clock or the hold?

choices.text: Destroys it, since the schedule's period is over
choices.why: The hold overrides every retention period; destroying evidence in a live case is exactly what it exists to stop.

choices.text: Asks IT to decide whether the case still matters
choices.why: A hold is placed and lifted by the people responsible for the case, not by IT.

choices.text: Moves it to cheaper storage and destroys it next year
choices.why: Next year the hold is still there unless legal lifts it; the move changes nothing about the rule.

choices.text: Skips it and waits for legal
choices.why: Right: in the lesson's case the hold is lifted in 2033 and the certificate goes in the run of January 2034.

prompt: About the 340 onboarding files of farms last paid years ago, Edson says: "Disk is cheap. Keep them, in case a farmer ever disputes a payment." What is the strongest answer?
hint: Whose data is in the file, and what justified keeping it?

choices.text: Agree, as long as the files are moved out of the main repository
choices.why: Moving personal data does not end its processing; the files would still hold a person's CPF and bank account with no reason left to keep them.

choices.text: Delete them right away and skip recording the disposal, so nothing is left
choices.why: The disposal itself is recorded, so that a later question about the file has an answer; leaving no trace is not the goal.

choices.text: No: the schedule's five years already cover that risk
choices.why: Right: the period was set for exactly this risk, and article 16 allows keeping personal data for a legal obligation, not for comfort. Past the date, keeping it breaks the rule.

choices.text: Keep them, because tax law makes every payment record permanent
choices.why: The payment records live under their own class, NF-e and tax books; the identity scans are a different class with its own period.

prompt: A certificate of analysis has just been declared a record. Which of these now hold for it? Choose all that apply.
hint: What changes when a document becomes evidence.

choices.text: Its author is refused if she tries to edit it
choices.why: Yes: a record is fixed, author included; a correction is a new document referring to it.

choices.text: Its retention period comes from the schedule's class for certificates
choices.why: Yes: five years from the end of the production year, at Serra Alta.

choices.text: An administrator is free to delete it to save space
choices.why: Declaring a record is what stops deletion, administrators included; space is not a reason in the schedule.

choices.text: A legal hold placed on it stops its disposal
choices.why: Yes: a hold overrides the retention period until the people handling the case lift it.

choices.text: When it is destroyed, no trace of it is left anywhere
choices.why: The disposal leaves its own record: what, under which rule, approved by whom, when.

prompt: Serra Alta bought EMC Documentum in 2010 and signed nothing new until its 2018 renewal. What changed in between?
hint: Look at the other side of the contract.

choices.text: The company on the other side of the contract, twice
choices.why: Right: Dell bought EMC in 2016 and OpenText bought the Documentum business in 2017; the servers and the software in the room stayed the same.

choices.text: The licence Serra Alta had already bought became invalid
choices.why: The licence already bought did not lapse; what moved was everything around it, from roadmap to support terms.

choices.text: Documentum was merged into OpenText's Content Server
choices.why: OpenText kept Documentum as a product and went on releasing it; the two repositories stayed separate products.

choices.text: Serra Alta's data moved to OpenText's servers
choices.why: Serra Alta runs Documentum in its own room; an acquisition of the vendor moves no customer data.

prompt: Why does it matter to Serra Alta that OpenText already had Content Server (formerly Livelink) when it bought Documentum?
hint: Two products, one owner, one budget.

choices.text: Content Server reads Documentum repositories directly, so no migration is needed
choices.why: Nothing in the lesson makes the two interchangeable; leaving one for the other is a migration like any other.

choices.text: The owner decides which of two competing products gets new features
choices.why: Right: a customer of a product with a sibling inside its owner asks where the investment goes, and does not assume it is their product.

choices.text: It forced Serra Alta to buy a Content Server licence
choices.why: The lesson describes no such obligation; the licence Serra Alta held stayed as it was.

choices.text: Nothing; a product line is a vendor's internal matter
choices.why: The roadmap is decided by the owner and lived with by the customer, which makes it the customer's concern too.

prompt: Serra Alta moves its repository to another product through CMIS. What arrives without further work, and what does not?
hint: CMIS covers the common ground and stops there.

choices.text: Everything arrives, because CMIS is a complete standard
choices.why: A standard of the common ground leaves out lifecycles, workflows and retention rules, and those hold most of the company's own work.

choices.text: Workflows arrive; the documents themselves have to be exported by hand
choices.why: It is the other way round: documents and properties are what the standard moves.

choices.text: Documents and properties; not lifecycles or retention rules
choices.why: Right: the process that governs the documents is outside CMIS and has to be configured again and tested.

choices.text: Nothing arrives until DQL is translated into the new product's language
choices.why: CMIS has its own query language and does not depend on DQL; that independence is its point.

prompt: Rui's team is rewriting the job that files certificates of analysis. Today it uses DFC and works perfectly. Following Joana's note, what should the new version be written against, and why?
hint: Think about the day the repository is replaced.

choices.text: DFC again, because it reaches every Documentum feature
choices.why: Reaching every feature is the problem: the job would be bound to Documentum's object model and rewritten when the repository is replaced.

choices.text: Direct SQL on the repository's database tables, for speed
choices.why: That binds the job to the product's internal schema, the tightest coupling of all, and skips the DMS's own checks.

choices.text: DQL, since it looks like SQL and any developer reads it
choices.why: Looking like SQL does not make it neutral: DQL speaks Documentum's object types and runs on Documentum alone.

choices.text: CMIS, so it outlives the repository
choices.why: Right: the neighbours of a replaceable repository speak a standard, and the certificate job is the first rewritten that way.

prompt: When the file server was replaced in 2019, the certificate paths stored in SAP's batch records stopped working. Why did nobody notice?
hint: What did SAP know about that field?

choices.text: The new server kept the old paths as redirects
choices.why: If it had, the paths would have kept working; they pointed at nothing.

choices.text: To SAP the path was free text, not a link it checked
choices.why: Right: a path is a string, and a string that stops meaning anything raises no error.

choices.text: The certificates had already been disposed of under the schedule
choices.why: Certificates from 2018 were well inside their five years in 2019; they existed and were simply unreachable.

choices.text: Documentum moved the files and updated SAP automatically
choices.why: The paths pointed at the file server, not at Documentum, and no system updated them.

prompt: Match each link to what it should store.
hint: Evidence points at what was true then; an instruction at what is true now.

pairs.left: a work order that says "work to the pasteurisation procedure"
the certificate sent to a customer last March
pairs.right: the object id of that exact version

pairs.left: finding a batch's certificates from inside the DMS
pairs.right: material and batch number as typed properties
the farm's vendor number from SAP

prompt: Why does the certificate carry the material as well as the batch number?
hint: How does SAP identify a batch?

choices.text: So the certificate's file name is unique
choices.why: The link does not rest on the file name at all; the properties are what a search reads.

choices.text: Because the customer asks by material, not by batch
choices.why: The supermarket asked by batch; the material is there because the batch number alone is not a key.

choices.text: SAP's key for a batch has two parts
choices.why: Right: use the whole key the ERP uses, or a search on the batch number one day returns two certificates.

choices.text: To decide its retention period
choices.why: The period for certificates counts from the end of the production year, whatever the material.

prompt: In Joana's design the DMS holds the batch key and SAP holds the document id. A check finds a batch in SAP pointing at a certificate whose properties name a different batch. Which side is trusted, and why?
hint: Which side was filled from the source, and which was copied?

choices.text: The DMS, set from the source at filing
choices.why: Right: a design that keeps a link in two places names one as the source of truth, and here it is the side written first, from the source.

choices.text: SAP, because the ERP is the system of record for everything
choices.why: SAP is the record for the batch; for this link the design names the DMS, whose properties were set at filing.

choices.text: Whichever was changed most recently
choices.why: The most recent change is as likely to be the mistake as the fix; the rule has to be decided before the disagreement.

choices.text: Neither; the certificate is deleted and generated again
choices.why: A certificate is a record and is not deleted to settle a mismatch; the link is corrected.

prompt: The ESB attaches the 300 KB certificate PDF to every order confirmation sent to two supermarket chains. Beyond queue size, what does the lesson hold against it?
hint: Count the copies, and ask who manages them.

choices.text: PDFs are not allowed inside SOAP messages
choices.why: A binary attachment is perfectly possible in a message; the objection is about records and access, not format.

choices.text: The customer receives the certificate later than with a link
choices.why: An attachment arrives with the message; speed is not the problem here.

choices.text: Attachments break the CMIS standard
choices.why: CMIS governs access to a repository; it says nothing about what an ESB carries.

choices.text: Each copy is an unmanaged record, outside retention, holds and the DMS's access checks
choices.why: Right: sending the id keeps one copy, checks access when it is fetched, and leaves retention to the DMS; lesson 11 calls it the claim check.

prompt: Joana writes the requirements for the new certificate job. Using the whole lesson, which belong on the list? Choose all that apply.
hint: One requirement each from records, the vendor section and linking.

choices.text: Declare each certificate a record at the moment it is filed
choices.why: Yes: the certificate is evidence from the start, fixed and under the schedule.

choices.text: Name each PDF after its batch so the lab finds it by searching
choices.why: That is today's half-measure; the batch belongs in typed properties, not in a name people retype.

choices.text: File it through CMIS with material, batch and plant as typed properties
choices.why: Yes: a standard interface and the whole business key.

choices.text: Write the new document's id back to the batch in SAP
choices.why: Yes: SAP then shows the certificate on the batch screen, with the DMS as the source of truth.

choices.text: Store the PDF's network path in the batch's long text as a fallback
choices.why: That is the link that silently broke in 2019; a fallback that breaks without a symptom is worse than none.

prompt: In January 2034 the disposal run destroys a certificate whose id is stored on a batch in SAP. What should happen to that link?
hint: The record of a disposal is kept for a reason.

choices.text: Leave it; a broken link shows the certificate is gone
choices.why: A link to nothing says nothing about why; it looks the same as a fault.

choices.text: Mark it disposed, with the date and the schedule's rule
choices.why: Right: the run reports the ids it destroyed and the link says so, for the same reason the disposal itself is recorded.

choices.text: Delete the batch from SAP as well
choices.why: The batch is a business record under its own rules; a certificate's disposal does not decide the batch's.

choices.text: Repoint it to the next version of the certificate
choices.why: A certificate has no next version that means the same thing; an evidence link names one exact version.

prompt: A work order has to open whichever version of POP-JF-PAS-004 is in force, so it stores the id of the version ___ rather than the id of one version.
hint: The word for all the versions of one document taken together.
